344.title: The bird on a string
344.hook: a bird on a string, a mind racing at 1am, and the self that goes home each night
344.carry: in deep sleep, the self goes home
344.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers use Uddalaka's tethered bird as an image for meditation on the breath, and the Upanishads' study of sleep, dream and deep sleep became a central theme in Vedanta.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: food, and the ember and the straw. The finest part of food becomes mind. Your line was the mind is made of food. Week three of year two begins.
screen: `FOOD — THE MIND IS MADE OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: Some nights your mind will not land. It's 1am and it's flying through tomorrow's meeting, last week's argument, a thing you said in seventh grade. Every direction, nowhere to rest. And then, at some point you never notice, it stops. You wake up and it's morning. Where did you go? Uddalaka has an answer, and it starts with a pun.
screen: `1AM, AND THE MIND WON'T LAND.` → `THEN, SOMEHOW, IT STOPS.` → `WHERE DID YOU GO?`

segments.voice: Learn from me about sleep, my dear, Uddalaka says. When a person sleeps, they become one with Being. They have gone to their own. He's playing on the Sanskrit. The word for he sleeps is svapiti. Uddalaka hears in it svam apita: gone to one's own. Sleep is going home. Then the picture. A bird tied by a string flies off this way, and that way, and every way, looking for somewhere else to rest, and finds nowhere. So in the end it settles down at the very place it's tied. The mind, he says, is just like that. It flies in every direction, finds no rest anywhere else, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Here's the teaching under the picture, one of the biggest in Hinduism. Your deepest self, the atman, isn't your racing thoughts. It is one with Being, sat, the reality under everything, and many teachers read this passage as saying that in deep, dreamless sleep you rest in it every night, without trying. Then, at the end of the lesson, Uddalaka says for the very first time the three words he'll keep repeating to his son: tat tvam asi. You are that. A handful of salt will open them in a few days. So, 1am, the mind flying through tomorrow's test and last week's argument: that's the bird pulling at its string. The worries are real, but they aren't you. Underneath them is a self that goes home every night.
screen: `SVAPITI: GONE TO ONE'S OWN.` · `A BIRD TIED BY A STRING.` · `THE ATMAN: NOT YOUR RACING THOUGHTS.` · `TAT TVAM ASI, FOR THE FIRST TIME.` · then, large: `THE SELF GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Let the mind fly wherever it wants for a few breaths, plans, worries, memories, and just watch it pull at the string. Then let it land: if you pray, on a name of God you love, said softly on each breath out; if you don't, on the breath itself. Each time it flies off, let it come back to where it's tied.
Sleep. In Uddalaka's teaching, going to one's own: the mind, like a tethered bird, comes to rest, and the self, the atman, goes home to Being.
screen: `SLEEP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in deep sleep, the self goes home. Tomorrow, the bees and the honey they make. Sleep well.

screen: `DAY 344 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BEES AND THE HONEY.`

345.title: The bees and the honey
345.hook: many trees, one honey: one Being under every creature, and each still itself
345.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep, the bird on a string coming back to where it's tied. Your line was in deep sleep, the self goes home.
screen: `SLEEP — THE SELF GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. Bees visited clover, dandelion, an apple tree, a lime tree, and plenty of flowers no one will ever list. They brought it all home and worked it together into one golden thing. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't. It's not gone; it's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.
screen: `WILDFLOWER HONEY.` → `CLOVER, DANDELION, APPLE, LIME.` → `FIND THE APPLE-TREE PART.`

segments.voice: Just as bees make honey, my dear, Uddalaka says, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way all these creatures, when they merge into Being, don't know: we have merged into Being. Then a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be. Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So hold both halves. Underneath, the separate names are gone: one Being, which later teachers call Brahman, under every creature. And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. That's the Hindu teaching in this jar: one reality under everything that lives, and each life still truly itself. Uddalaka isn't erasing anyone. It's one reason Hindu teachers ask you to see the sacred in every creature, not just the ones you like. The kid at school who gets on your nerves, the neighbor's barking dog, the mosquito at your ear: different jars, the same sweetness underneath. Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.
screen: `MANY JUICES, ONE SWEETNESS.` · `NO JUICE SAYS: I'M FROM THIS TREE.` · `THE TIGER WAKES UP A TIGER.` · `ONE BEING UNDER EVERY CREATURE.` · then, large: `ONE BEING UNDER EVERY NAME.`

segments.voice: Pick out the separate sounds around you one at a time, a fan, a car outside, a voice, your own breath, and name each one. Then, breath by breath, stop naming them, and let them run together into one sound, no part saying where it came from.
Madhu, honey, sweetness. Many juices, one sweetness: in Being, no creature says I came from this tree, and in the world, each comes back as itself.
screen: `MADHU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one Being under every name, and every name still itself. Tomorrow, the rivers. See you then.

346.title: The rivers and the sea
346.hook: rivers rise from the sea and run back to it: where we come from, and where we go
346.carry: we come from Being, and go back
346.tomorrow: the tree: cut it, it bleeds
346.howItsDone: Rivers are sacred for many Hindus, who bathe in them on festival days and immerse ashes after cremation; Vedanta teachers often use Uddalaka's rivers and the sea to describe the relation of the self to Brahman.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhu, many juices, one sweetness. Your line was one Being under every name. Today, the rivers.
screen: `MADHU — ONE BEING UNDER EVERY NAME.`

segments.voice: Rivers have names, and people love those names. They write songs about them, fight over them, scatter ashes in them, bathe in them on holy days. The Ganga, the Yamuna, the Mississippi, the Thames. A river has a source, a path, a personality: slow and brown, or fast and cold. Then it reaches the sea. Stand on a beach and look out. Which part of that water was the Ganga? Uddalaka asks his son the same thing.
screen: `RIVERS HAVE NAMES.` → `SONGS, ASHES, HOLY DAYS.` → `WHICH PART WAS THE GANGA?`

segments.voice: These rivers, my dear, Uddalaka says, the eastern ones flow toward the east, the western ones toward the west. They go from sea to sea. They become the sea itself. And there, in the sea, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Notice that little phrase, from sea to sea. Commentators hear the water cycle in it: water rises from the sea as cloud, falls as rain, gathers into rivers, and runs back home. The river was the sea all along, on a long walk. Then he turns it around. In the same way, my dear, all these creatures, though they have come from Being, don't know: we have come from Being. Here is the teaching, and it runs all through Hinduism: everything comes out of Being, the one reality later teachers call Brahman, and everything goes back to it. A life is a river, truly itself while it runs, and never cut off from the sea it came from. And Uddalaka says again, whatever they are here, tiger or lion or gnat, they become that. Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world; you are that, Shvetaketu. Some Vedanta schools hear the river as finally nothing but sea. Others hear it as a real, beloved part of the sea. Either way, when someone you love is near the end, this teaching doesn't say they'll vanish. It says the river is going home.
screen: `EAST AND WEST, FROM SEA TO SEA.` · `THEY DON'T KNOW: I AM THIS RIVER.` · `EVERYTHING COMES FROM BEING, AND GOES BACK.` · `THE RIVER IS GOING HOME.` · then, large: `THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Picture a river you know and start at its source, a spring in the hills; on each breath, let it run a little farther, past towns and under bridges, wider and slower. Then let it reach the sea, and rest in the open water without needing to know which part was which.
Samudra, the sea, the gathering of waters. Rivers flow from sea to sea, become the sea, and there don't say I am this river; so creatures come from Being and don't know it.
screen: `SAMUDRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: we come from Being, and go back. Every river was on its way home. Day three hundred forty-six, done.

347.title: The tree that bleeds and lives
347.hook: strike a great tree anywhere and it lives; why Hindus say the self does not die
347.carry: the body dies; the self does not
347.howItsDone: At Hindu deathbeds and funerals, families may recite or reflect on scriptures that teach that the self does not die with the body, from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: samudra, rivers that run from sea to sea. Your line was we come from Being, and go back.
screen: `SAMUDRA — WE COME FROM BEING, AND GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Find an old tree with a scar: where a branch was cut, or a car hit it, or someone carved initials years ago. Often you'll see where the sap ran, dried now into a hard, shiny crust. The tree bled. And it's still standing, still leafing out every spring. Next to it, maybe, one branch is gray and bare, and never came back. Same tree. One part alive, one part not. Uddalaka points his son to a great tree.
screen: `AN OLD TREE WITH A SCAR.` → `IT BLED, AND IT'S STILL STANDING.` → `ONE GRAY BRANCH.`

segments.voice: If someone were to strike this great tree at its root, my dear, Uddalaka says, it would bleed sap, but it would live. Strike it in the middle, it would bleed, but live. Strike it at the top, it would bleed, but live. Filled through and through by the living self, the jiva atman, it stands, drinking in water, rejoicing. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves a second, or a third, they dry up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. Then the line that turns it toward his son. In the same way, my dear, understand this: the body dies when life leaves it. But life does not die. Look at the order. The body depends on the self, not the other way around. A dry branch isn't the death of life; it's life leaving that branch. This is one of Hinduism's central teachings: the atman, the self, is not the body, and it does not die. The Bhagavad Gita says it too, in its second chapter: as a person puts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body. That is the hope many Hindu families hold onto at a funeral. They grieve, truly. And they say: the body has died; the one we love has not. Then the refrain once more: you are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `STRIKE IT: IT BLEEDS, BUT LIVES.` · `LIFE LEAVES A BRANCH; IT DRIES.` · `THE ATMAN IS NOT THE BODY.` · `WORN-OUT CLOTHES, PUT OFF.` · then, large: `THE BODY DIES. THE SELF DOES NOT.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your feet, your roots, and feel something alive there: warmth, tingling, a pulse. Move up through your belly and chest, where the breath moves, to your face and scalp, the same life from root to crown, and rest in it the way the tree stands, drinking in water.
The tree. Uddalaka's great tree, filled by the living self: wounded, it lives; when life leaves, it dries; the body dies, but the self does not.

348.title: The banyan seed
348.hook: break a seed, see nothing, and learn what holds up the whole tree
348.carry: the unseen essence holds up the world
348.howItsDone: The banyan is sacred to many Hindus and is often worshipped, especially by women during the Vat Savitri festival; teachers use Uddalaka's banyan seed to explain the subtle essence behind the visible world.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tree, struck at root, middle and top, bleeding but alive. Your line was the body dies; the self does not.
screen: `THE TREE — THE BODY DIES. THE SELF DOES NOT.`

segments.voice: A banyan doesn't stop at one trunk. It sends roots down from its branches, and those roots thicken into new trunks, until one tree can look like a small forest. Birds nest in it, people sit in its shade, and all of it is one tree. Its fruit is a little fig a bird could swallow whole, with seeds like specks of dust inside. Uddalaka sends his son to fetch one.
screen: `A TREE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FOREST.` → `ROOTS THAT BECOME TRUNKS.` → `IT STARTED AS A TINY SEED.`

segments.voice: The lesson is a short conversation, almost a game. Bring me a fruit from that banyan. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. It's broken, sir. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And the father says: my dear, that subtle essence you can't see, from that very essence this great banyan tree stands. Believe me, my dear. He doesn't describe the seed. He has his son break it with his own hands and look, and the son reports honestly: nothing. That nothing is the point. Not empty nothing. Too-fine-to-see nothing. Uddalaka's word is anima, the subtlest. Here is the Hindu teaching: what's most real isn't the biggest thing in the room. It's the unseen essence that everything you can see stands on. Then he asks for shraddha, faith: shraddhatsva, believe me. Not belief instead of looking; his son has just looked as hard as anyone can. In this story, faith comes after looking, at the edge of what eyes can do. So when a classmate asks, where's God, under a microscope? Uddalaka's son already tried that with a seed. Look as closely as you like. The tree is still standing. Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. You are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` · `WHAT DO YOU SEE? NOTHING AT ALL.` · `ANIMA: THE SUBTLEST.` · `SHRADDHA: FAITH, AFTER LOOKING.` · then, large: `FROM THAT, THIS GREAT TREE.`

segments.voice: Start with something big in your life, your body, your family, your work, and go smaller, the way the son broke the fruit and then the seed: what's this made of, and that? When you reach the edge of what you can see, don't force an answer; rest there.
Anima, the subtlest, the finest. Broken open, the banyan seed shows nothing at all; from that unseen, subtle essence, the father says, the great banyan stands.
screen: `ANIMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the unseen essence holds up the world. From that, this great tree stands. Until tomorrow.

349.title: Salt in water
349.hook: salt you can't find, salty in every sip: the three words 'you are that'
349.carry: tat tvam asi: you are that
349.howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and in some traditions it is taught to monks at their initiation; each Vedanta school has its own commentary on it.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: anima, the seed broken open, and nothing at all inside. Your line was the unseen essence holds up the world.
screen: `ANIMA — THE UNSEEN ESSENCE HOLDS UP THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Take a glass of water and a pinch of salt. Drop the salt in, and watch the grains sink, cloud and disappear. Leave it overnight. In the morning, try to pick the salt back out. You can't. It isn't anywhere you can point to. And yet you know it's in there, and you know exactly how to find out. This is Uddalaka's most famous lesson, where his three-word refrain lands with full weight.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER, A PINCH OF SALT.` → `IN THE MORNING, PICK IT OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T. BUT IT'S THERE.`

segments.voice: Put this salt in water, Uddalaka says, and come to me in the morning. Shvetaketu does. In the morning his father says: bring me the salt you put in last night. He looks, and can't find it; it has dissolved. Sip from this end. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the far end? Salty. Then, the father says, you don't see Being here, my dear, but it is truly here. That subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. Tat tvam asi, Shvetaketu. You are that. Those three words are among the most famous in Hindu scripture. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. Later teachers counted them among the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, of the Upanishads. The honey and the rivers showed the names dissolving. The seed showed the essence too fine to see. The salt shows it's everywhere at once, in every sip, every drop. And the schools of Vedanta hear the three words differently. Shankara's Advaita hears pure identity: your deepest self and Being are one. Ramanuja hears the self as real and distinct, yet belonging to Brahman, the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita school reads the same Sanskrit with a different word break, as atat tvam asi: you are not that, not the same as the Lord. All of them taste the same water. And here's why the words matter on an ordinary day: if Being is in every sip, it is in the person across the table too. That's the root of the Hindu habit of seeing the sacred in the one you meet.

350.title: The blindfolded man
350.hook: a man left blindfolded far from home, and why Hindus honor the one who unties it
350.carry: the guru unties the blindfold; you walk
350.tomorrow: the dying man and the fire ordeal
350.howItsDone: Hindu traditions give the guru, the teacher, a place of honor, and many communities observe Guru Purnima each year to give thanks to their teachers.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Being, unseen yet truly here, like salt in water. Your line was tat tvam asi: you are that. Today ends week three of year two.
screen: `BEING — TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Honey and rivers, trees and seeds and salt. And still, maybe, Shvetaketu is thinking what anyone would think. Fine. Being is everywhere, and I am that. So why don't I feel it? Why am I still lost? His father doesn't scold him, and doesn't repeat the salt one more time. He tells him about a man led far from home with a cloth tied over his eyes.
screen: `HONEY, RIVERS, TREES, SEEDS, SALT.` → `SO WHY DON'T I FEEL IT?` → `A MAN WITH A CLOTH OVER HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Suppose, Uddalaka says, someone leads a man away from his home in Gandhara with his eyes covered, and leaves him in a lonely, empty place. The man turns and shouts, east, north, south: I was brought here blindfolded and left here blindfolded! Then someone unties the cloth and says: Gandhara is that way. Go. And the man, asking from village to village, informed and thinking for himself, gets all the way home. In the same way, Uddalaka says, a person who has a teacher knows. Look at who does what. The stranger doesn't carry the man home. He takes off the blindfold and points. The man still has to walk, and ask, and use his own head. And Gandhara was there the whole time; he just couldn't see which way to turn. Uddalaka adds that for such a person, the only delay is until he's released from the body; then he arrives. And the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. Here's the teaching, and it's why Hinduism honors the guru so highly. All week, Being was in the honey, the rivers, the seed, the salt, and in you. What's missing isn't the road; it's sight. A guru unties the blindfold. That's why many Hindus bow to a teacher, touch their feet, and give thanks on Guru Purnima: not because the teacher walks for you, but because they showed you which way home is.
screen: `BLINDFOLDED AND LEFT ALONE.` · `SOMEONE UNTIES IT AND POINTS.` · `HE ASKS, VILLAGE BY VILLAGE.` · `WHY HINDUS HONOR THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE WITH A TEACHER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who untied a blindfold for you, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, and see their face; remember what they said or did. They didn't walk the road for you; they pointed, and you walked. Many Hindus bow to a teacher; if you'd like, bow your head to them in your mind, and let gratitude rise if it's there.
Acharyavan, one who has a teacher. Untied and pointed toward Gandhara, he asks his way village by village; so one who has a teacher knows.
